source.title: Guiding Giants: Lightweight Controllers for Weighted Activation Steering in LLMs
source.authors: Amr Hegazy; Mostafa Elhoushi; Amr Alanwar

record.file_problem: The paper is present in full. Some embedded figure text is garbled, but the reported tables and main text are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a precomputed refusal steering vector as part of its own adaptive safety controller and evaluates that controller. Its vector is derived from output-token embeddings, not harmful-minus-harmless mean activations, and it does not test the original direction by ablating or adding it as specified in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports WAS refusal and capability outcomes, including variations in steering strength and layer range. These are results for its own controller and token-embedding-derived vector, not tests of the claim’s difference-in-means direction. The method’s training on harmful and benign prompts does not compare training setups or test whether a single removable refusal direction exists. The judge prompt and the quoted CumGPT example are methodological/example prompts, not instructions to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study builds an adaptive steering controller (WAS) around a fixed 'refusal direction' made from output-embedding contrasts of refusal tokens versus answer tokens. It is not the harmful-minus-harmless activation mean. The study reports only its own method's refusal and capability performance against base models and other steering methods. It never ablates a direction, never tests a difference-in-means direction, and never examines whether refusal is mediated by one direction, so none of V1–V8 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude WAS greatly increases refusal on harmful benchmarks while preserving benign performance, as a low-overhead inference-time safety layer. They note limits: dependence on the steering vector's quality, hyperparameter sensitivity, generalization concerns, and the controller itself as an attack surface.
record.recipe_differences: WAS derives its fixed vector by contrasting mean output embeddings of refusal-related and answer-related tokens, and applies it through a learned prompt-conditioned scalar and per-layer weights. It does not use the claimed harmful-minus-harmless activation-mean direction or test its ablation/addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported WAS outcomes vary with global patch scale and the selected layer range; the paper also reports different results for scalar-only versus scalar-plus-layer-weight control.

fits_no_version.finding: A learned controller applying a token-embedding refusal-vs-answer vector with per-prompt scale and per-layer weights raises refusal on ToxicChat, In-The-Wild Jailbreak and AdvBench over the base model in Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B and Mistral-7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive, prompt-gated addition of an output-embedding refusal vector increases refusal on harmful-prompt benchmarks.

fits_no_version.finding: At αglobal=2.0, the AlpacaEval win rate is about 50% versus base, with small MMLU drops (e.g. 63.0→60.8) and a HellaSwag drop for Mistral (69.8→65.4). Utility falls at higher scale (42.1% at α=4.0).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: WAS largely preserves benign-task utility at the chosen scale; utility depends on scale and model.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal under WAS depends on the learned layer weights, the layers patched (late 81.2% vs early 52.4% vs all 93.0%), and the global scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For additive refusal steering, outcomes depend on layer allocation and strength.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 6th Workshop on Trustworthy NLP (TrustNLP 2026)
record.problems: The refusal-rate tables do not state uncertainty estimates. Evaluation uses the paper’s keyword-based refusal detector with GPT-4o as a secondary judge, and the paper does not report a control applying a random or otherwise unrelated direction. Its own limitations note dependence on the precomputed vector, sensitivity to patch scale, possible overfitting or poor generalization, and vulnerability to adversarial prompts targeting the controller.
record.rows_left_out: Did not extract CAST, ACT, and ITI comparator scores from Table 1 because they are other methods rather than outcomes of the refusal vector used by this study. Did not extract inference-time latency values from Figure 3 because they are figure-only and do not measure refusal or capability. Other figure-only controller-weight visualizations are not refusal or capability outcome measures.

untested.parts: No harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation direction is built; no ablation; addition uses an output-embedding token-contrast vector gated by a learned controller, with no test of harmless-prompt refusal induction.
Jailbreak prompts are used only as a benchmark; there is no analysis of whether attacks suppress a refusal direction, and no adversarial training against ablation.
Single versus multiple directions is not examined; the layer-weight patterns concern the steering allocation of one fixed vector.
The controller discriminates harmful from benign activations, but the separation of harm encoding from the refusal direction is not tested.
No transfer across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models; the authors say the controller is unlikely to transfer across models.

record.verdict_notes: The term 'refusal direction' here is not the original's difference-in-means activation direction. It is built from unembedding rows of refusal versus answer phrases, following ActAdd-style contrast. There is no random-vector control. The base-model AdvBench refusal for Mistral (10.2%) is reported as is. Rows r28, r35, r42, r46 and r51 duplicate the main results with self-referential baselines. All rows are correctly linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless activation-mean direction is constructed or tested; no ablation of that direction or addition intended to cause refusals to harmless requests is reported.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
Jailbreak prompts are evaluated, but the study does not test whether attacks suppress the claimed direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The study does not test whether refusal is encoded by an affine set, cone, or multiple directions.
No separate representation of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision is tested.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer of the claimed direction is tested.
The controller is trained on harmful and benign prompt activations, but the study does not compare training regimes or test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.
